source.title: Beyond Harmful Fine-Tuning: Evaluating Open-Weight Safeguards Under Training-Free Tampering

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a harmful-minus-harmless contrastive refusal direction and removes it during inference, then measures harmful-response rates, directly applying the original direction-ablation approach.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal-ablation results and ablation combined with prompt tampering. Prompt-only results are not rows because they do not apply or measure the direction. The PCA and token-level KL diagnostics are recorded as findings not covered by a claim version. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study applies Arditi-style difference-in-means refusal-direction ablation at inference, via ABLITERIX, to three models not in the original work. Two of them carry safeguards (SEAM, Safety Pretraining). It reports harmful-response rates for standalone ablation against default chat, so its results bear on whether ablating the direction removes refusal in this new setting. It is not T1: the measure is judged harmful-compliance ASR, not refusal score, and layer/position choices are not reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that prompt-level tampering (especially prefilling) and refusal ablation substantially raise harmful responses, including in SEAM and Safety-Pretraining models. They argue that fine-tuning robustness is not tamper-resistance and call for tiered prompt/representation/weight evaluations before release.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless contrastive refusal direction and removes it at inference, following Arditi et al. via ABLITERIX. The paper does not specify its layer and token-position choices or report an addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, benchmark, and tampering composition. The paper reports different ASRs for standalone ablation and ablation combined with system prompting, prefilling, or both.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeLM-1.7B-Instruct keeps harmful/harmless separability in 2D PCA at layer 16/24. Its KL divergence from SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct on harmful continuations concentrates at the first response token.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety Pretraining leaves separable harmful-vs-harmless structure and shallow first-token safety concentration.

record.problems: ASR values come from a single deterministic greedy-decoding run, without multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates. The paper describes the refusal-ablation pipeline as fixed but does not specify its layer and token-position configuration in the provided text. It does not test general capability after ablation or compare directions, and the authors characterize the attacks as proof-of-concept rather than worst-case.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported ablation or diagnostic results were left out. Prompt-only attack results were excluded because they do not apply or measure the refusal direction.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; preservation of other abilities after ablation; layer/position selection (not reported); refusal-score measure as in the original.
Weight orthogonalization is only mentioned as possible; no weight edit is run.
Whether jailbreaks (including the prefill attack) act by suppressing the direction; adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison with multi-direction, cone or affine accounts.
Harm judgment vs refusal decision not separated; the PCA separability is not a test of this.
No transfer of a direction across languages, variants or base/instruct.

Ablation is applied to SEAM and safety-pretrained models, but is not compared against unprotected counterparts (the SEAM-vs-base comparison covers only fine-tuning and prompt attacks). Training effects on the direction are therefore not isolated.
Qwen3.5-9B is run in non-thinking mode; no reasoning models are tested.

record.verdict_notes: Ablation results come from a single greedy run with no uncertainty estimates and no capability check. The authors call the attacks proof-of-concept, with no search over layers, positions or strength, so the incompleteness may reflect configuration rather than mechanism. ASR here is judged harmful compliance (StrongREJECT evaluator, WildGuard), which is stricter than the original's refusal-absence measure. Combination rows are kept linked to V1 as cannot_determine. One could estimate ablation's added effect by comparing them with their prompt-only counterparts, but the paper does not frame them that way.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests removal, not adding the direction. It does not assess whether other abilities remain intact, and does not state that the direction is projected out at every layer and position.
The paper mentions converting refusal ablation into a modified checkpoint, but does not run or evaluate a weight edit.
The study applies ablation as an attack, but does not test whether other jailbreaks suppress this direction or whether training against ablation adds robustness.
It does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account of refusal.
It does not distinguish harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
It applies ablation to different models, but does not test whether a direction transfers across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
It evaluates ablation on models with different safeguards, but does not isolate how or when training determines whether one removable direction exists.
It does not evaluate reasoning models.

labels.condition: Standalone inference-time ablation on all three models (Qwen3.5-9B, SEAM Llama-3.2-3B, SafeLM-1.7B), both benchmarks
labels.reason: All six ASR rows for this group are partial: ablation raises ASR from 0.48-12.50% to only 33.10-71.56%, so 28-67% of responses are still not judged harmful. That is incomplete removal, which is limits_scope. The supports and limits_scope verdicts cover the same condition group. Merge them into one limits_scope: the effect is clear on all three models, including the safeguarded ones, but incomplete under this fixed setup.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Fixed, untuned ABLITERIX configuration; judged harmful-compliance ASR
labels.reason: The label is right: ablation leaves most responses not harmful on Qwen StrongREJECT (33.10%) and Llama StrongREJECT (40.97%). Two details in the reason are off. 'No stronger than prefilling on StrongREJECT' holds for Qwen (33.10 vs 35.86) and Llama (40.97 vs 43.16) but not SafeLM (52.62 vs 49.07). L-HB-A (50.62%) is not a 'most non-harmful' cell.

relation.reason: Table 1 reports standalone refusal ablation against default chat on all three models. These are the study's own results on whether ablating the direction removes refusal.

tranche.reason: Arditi-style difference-in-means ablation, run via ABLITERIX with unreported layer and position, is applied to three new models, two of them safeguarded. The measure is judged harmful-response ASR on StrongREJECT and HarmBench (WildGuard), not Arditi's refusal and safety scores. So T3 (a new setting with a result) fits better than T1.

source_check.notes: The pack lists no [lN] ids, so l1 and l2 were assigned in listed order. Possible missing V7 verdict: SEAM and Safety Pretraining (training-stage safeguards) do not stop ablation (ASR 40.97-58.75%). Figure 2's PCA (layer 16 of 24, 512 pairs) is correlational only. Untested: no capability measure, no random-direction control, no induction by adding the direction, no weight edit (V2 is only discussed).

statements.correction: Qwen3.5-9B: StrongREJECT ASR 3.39% -> 33.10%, HarmBench ASR 12.50% -> 71.56% (chat -> refusal ablation, Table 1). All Qwen3.5-9B evaluations were in non-thinking mode (B.5). Layer and token position are not reported ('a chosen layer and token position', ABLITERIX). Refusal-ablation settings are fixed with no hyperparameter search. One deterministic greedy run, max_new_tokens 1024. Judges: the official StrongREJECT evaluator, and safety-eval with WildGuard for HarmBench. ASR is the harmful-response rate, not a refusal rate.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right, but the claim that it does not report reasoning mode is wrong. Appendix B.5 says Qwen3.5-9B was run in non-thinking mode. This matters because the conflict sets it against 2605.21706, which tags the model as reasoning.
